## Report Header

Filing institution: Cortex Bank and Trust
Internal case reference: FIU-2024-1736
Report filed: December 11, 2024
Suspected activity: structuring / CTR avoidance
Risk tier: medium
Subjects of this report:
  Beatriz Zimmerman (individual), account 57-21534-1
  Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC (business), account 88-53482-2
  Benedict Tillingham (individual), account 34-72893-3
  Séverin Castellanos (individual), account 15-57913-4
  Philippa Ashworth (individual), account 36-56838-5
Review period: December 18, 2023 through November 1, 2024
Aggregate amount of activity reviewed: $899,468.70

## Activity Overview

The Cortex Bank and Trust Financial Intelligence Unit initiated a review of customer Beatriz Zimmerman (account 57-21534-1) following a referral from branch personnel regarding unusual cash handling practices. The review period for this investigation spans from December 18, 2023, through November 1, 2024. The activity under review primarily involves suspected attempts to evade Currency Transaction Report requirements through the systematic structuring of cash deposits. The aggregate cash volume deposited into the subject account during the review period was $899,468.70.

The activity was characterized by a sustained pattern of cash deposits falling just below the $10,000 regulatory reporting threshold. A significant concentration of these deposits occurred within a narrow band, frequently between $9,719.68 and $8,917.00. These transactions were consistently executed across various Cortex Bank and Trust branch locations, often involving multiple branches within the same business day or on consecutive days. The branch referral that prompted this review noted that the subject made specific inquiries at the teller line regarding the bank's reporting obligations for cash transactions, further suggesting an awareness of and intent to circumvent these thresholds.

During the initial phase of the review period, a concentrated sequence of deposits was observed. For example, on December 26, 2023, a deposit of $8,861.79 was credited to the account. This was followed on December 27, 2023, by another sub-threshold deposit of $8,402.48 at a different branch location. A subsequent deposit of $9,344.10 was recorded on December 28, 2023, at yet another branch. This pattern of consecutive, sub-threshold deposits across varying locations is indicative of structuring behavior designed to avoid triggering a CTR while introducing substantial cash volumes into the financial system.

The funds deposited in this manner did not remain in the account for any significant duration. The review identified a consistent pattern wherein the aggregated cash deposits were rapidly depleted through outbound transfers. These transfers were often executed shortly after the deposits cleared, sometimes on the same day or the following business day. The outbound transfers were frequently directed to counterparties, including Driftwood Logistics Holdings Ltd., Orchard Gate Ventures Enterprises LLC, and Thistledown Commodities Partners LP.

The velocity of funds moving through the account was notable. The rapid succession of cash deposits followed by outbound transfers suggests the account may be functioning as a conduit for moving funds rather than for customary personal or business banking purposes. The outbound activity included significant sums, with the largest single outbound transfer during the review period amounting to $202,783.80. This transfer, directed to Cascadia Consulting Corp., occurred after a period of accumulated sub-threshold cash deposits, indicating a potential consolidation of the structured funds before their onward transmission.

Further analysis of the account activity revealed interactions with other entities, including Quarrystone Textiles Inc., Cedarline Ventures Corp., and Fairmount Holdings Partners LP. The nature of the relationships between the subject and these counterparties, as well as the economic purpose of the transfers, remains unclear based on the transactional data alone. The frequency and volume of these transfers, coupled with the structured nature of the funding deposits, present a heightened risk profile.

The pattern of branch rotation was a key element of the suspected structuring activity. By utilizing different branch locations, sometimes on the same day, the subject appeared to be attempting to obscure the total volume of cash being deposited from any single teller or branch manager. This tactic, when combined with the sub-threshold deposit amounts, is a recognized method for avoiding detection and circumventing CTR reporting requirements.

The inquiries made by the subject at the teller line regarding reporting thresholds further corroborate the suspicion of intentional structuring. Such inquiries demonstrate a level of knowledge regarding anti-money laundering regulations and suggest a deliberate effort to structure transactions in a manner that avoids triggering those regulations.

The activity observed in the account of Beatriz Zimmerman presents several indicators consistent with structuring to evade CTR requirements. The high volume of cash deposits, the consistent sub-threshold amounts, the rapid movement of funds out of the account, and the apparent use of the account as a pass-through entity all contribute to the suspicious nature of the activity. The utilization of multiple branch locations and the subject's inquiries regarding reporting thresholds further underscore the potential intent to circumvent regulatory reporting.

The review of the account activity for the period from December 18, 2023, to November 1, 2024, indicates a sustained pattern of behavior that warrants further investigation. The aggregate cash volume of $899,468.70, introduced primarily through sub-threshold deposits, represents a significant influx of funds whose source and ultimate destination require closer scrutiny. The rapid depletion of these funds through outbound transfers to various counterparties adds a layer of complexity to the transactional profile and raises questions regarding the legitimate business purpose of the account activity. The subsequent sections of this report will delve into specific transaction sequences, counterparty relationships, and the overall economic rationale for the observed behavior.

## Subject Background and Relationship History

Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC established a commercial banking relationship with Cortex Bank and Trust on December 18, 2023. The subject opened a single product, a commercial checking account, identified as account 88-53482-2. The account was established at a retail branch location, with an individual acting as the authorized signor. At the time of onboarding, the subject declared its primary business activity as the wholesale export of agricultural and forestry commodities, with a focus on serving clients in the Pacific Northwest and western Canada. The subject's stated business address was located in an industrial park within the bank's assessment area. 

The customer risk profile, completed at account opening, anticipated moderate transaction volumes consistent with a newly established wholesale enterprise. Expected activity included wire transfers, both domestic and international, for the payment of suppliers and the receipt of funds from overseas buyers. The expected monthly volume for these wire transfers was projected in the low six-figure range. The subject also indicated an expectation of routine automated clearing house activity for payroll and vendor payments, along with a minimal volume of check deposits. Crucially, the initial risk profile did not anticipate significant cash activity. The authorized signor explicitly stated that the business model did not involve retail sales or over-the-counter cash transactions, and that cash deposits would be infrequent and immaterial to the overall operation. Based on the provided information, the industry type, and the expected transaction profile, Cortex Bank and Trust assigned Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC a low initial risk rating.

A review of the account activity from inception through the early stages of the review period revealed a substantial deviation from the expected profile. While the account did experience the anticipated wire transfer activity, the volume and frequency of cash deposits were entirely inconsistent with the declared business model of a wholesale commodities exporter. Within days of account opening, specifically beginning on December 20, 2023, the account began receiving substantial cash deposits. These deposits were not the infrequent, immaterial amounts initially described; rather, they formed the primary source of funding for the account. The volume of cash activity rapidly escalated, contradicting the expected low-volume profile. The aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period reached $899,468.70, an amount fundamentally incompatible with the stated expectations for a business operating in the wholesale export sector. 

The nature of the cash deposits further contradicted the expected activity. The deposits were consistently structured in amounts just below the $10,000 currency transaction reporting threshold. This pattern of sub-threshold deposits, including individual transactions of $8,861.79, $8,402.48, and $9,344.10, is not characteristic of routine business receipts. The clustering of these deposits between $9,719.68 and $8,917.00 strongly suggested an intent to evade the reporting requirements associated with large cash transactions. 

Furthermore, the timing and location of these deposits presented significant anomalies. The deposits were frequently made on consecutive business days, and on several occasions, multiple deposits were made on the same day at different Cortex Bank and Trust branch locations. This branch rotation strategy, observed on December 26, 2023, December 27, 2023, and December 28, 2023, further indicated a deliberate effort to conceal the true volume of cash being introduced into the financial system and to avoid triggering internal aggregate reporting mechanisms. On December 29, 2023, the reviewing analyst noted documentation in the customer interaction log indicating that the individual conducting the deposits inquired about the bank's currency transaction reporting thresholds at the teller line, a behavior often associated with structuring activity.

The disposition of the funds also deviated from the expected profile. The initial risk assessment anticipated wire transfers directed toward international buyers and domestic suppliers. However, the observed activity demonstrated a pattern of rapid, high-velocity outward transfers following the cash deposits. These outbound transfers, including a notable transaction of $202,783.80, were frequently directed to counterparties not identified during onboarding and whose relationship to the subject's stated line of business was unclear. The rapid movement of funds, often occurring on the same day or the day following the cash deposits, is consistent with the placement and layering phases of money laundering, rather than routine business operations. 

The counterparties receiving these outbound transfers included entities such as Driftwood Logistics Holdings Ltd., Orchard Gate Ventures Enterprises LLC, and Thistledown Commodities Partners LP. While the names of these entities suggest a potential connection to logistics or commodities, independent research failed to confirm their legitimate business operations or their relationship to Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC. The flow of funds to these entities, particularly following significant, structured cash deposits, raised concerns regarding the true nature of the transactions.

The stark contrast between the declared business model of a wholesale commodities exporter and the observed activity of high-volume, structured cash deposits followed by rapid outbound transfers prompted a reassessment of the subject's risk profile. The activity is not consistent with the typical financial behavior of a business operating in the stated industry, nor does it align with the expectations established at account opening. The subject was unable to substantiate the source of the significant cash deposits, and no legitimate business purpose was identified for the complex pattern of transactions. The observed activity, characterized by potential structuring, branch rotation, and the rapid movement of funds to unexplained counterparties, indicates a significantly higher level of risk than initially assessed.

## Account Profile and Baseline Activity - Benedict Tillingham

Account 34-72893-3 was established by Benedict Tillingham in his individual capacity on a date preceding the current review period. At account opening, the customer profile recorded Benedict Tillingham’s occupation as a freelance consultant specializing in logistics optimization. Expected account activity detailed at onboarding included recurring direct deposits from client engagements, occasional wire transfers for business expenses, and routine debit card transactions for personal expenditures. The anticipated cash volume was designated as minimal, reflecting the typical financial behavior of a professional service provider.

Prior to the commencement of the review period on December 18, 2023, the account exhibited a pattern of transaction activity consistent with the established customer profile. Monthly credit volume was characterized by a series of electronic deposits, primarily automated clearing house credits, originating from a consistent set of counterparties. The debit activity was similarly routine, consisting predominantly of point-of-sale transactions, recurring automated payments for utilities and services, and occasional check disbursements. The account maintained an average monthly balance in the mid-five figures, and the transaction velocity remained relatively stable month over month.

The statistical baseline maintained by the transaction monitoring system for Account 34-72893-3 reflected this consistent pattern of activity. The system recorded an average monthly cash deposit volume of a low four-figure sum, with individual cash deposits rarely exceeding several hundred dollars. The baseline for outgoing funds transfers was established at a moderate level, consistent with the anticipated business expenses. The monitoring system also established a baseline for the frequency and geographic dispersion of transactions, which indicated a localized pattern of activity centered around Benedict Tillingham’s stated residence and business address.

The activity observed during the review period, commencing on December 18, 2023, represented a significant deviation from the established statistical baseline. The most prominent anomaly was a sudden and substantial increase in the volume and frequency of cash deposits. This shift in behavior was initially detected by the transaction monitoring system, which generated alerts based on the velocity and aggregate value of the cash credits.

The review-period activity was characterized by a pattern of frequent cash deposits, often occurring on consecutive business days. The aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period was $899,468.70. This figure represents a dramatic escalation compared to the historical baseline of minimal cash activity. The deposits were consistently structured in amounts falling just below the $10,000 threshold for currency transaction reporting.

An analysis of the individual transactions revealed a pattern of deposits clustered between $9,719.68 and $8,917.00. For instance, on a date during the review period, a cash deposit of $8,861.79 was recorded. On another date, a cash deposit of $8,402.48 was transacted. A third deposit of $9,344.10 was also noted. These amounts, while individually below the reporting threshold, collectively constituted a substantial volume of cash entering the account within a compressed timeframe.

The timing and location of these deposits further deviated from the expected behavior. The transactions were frequently conducted across multiple branch locations within the Cortex Bank and Trust network. On several occasions, deposits were made at different branches on the same business day or on consecutive days, a practice commonly referred to as branch rotation. This behavior is often associated with attempts to evade detection or circumvent internal controls by dispersing activity across different points of contact.

The deviation from the baseline extended beyond the cash deposits. The outbound transaction activity also exhibited significant changes during the review period. The account, which previously demonstrated routine debit activity, began to execute large outgoing funds transfers. These transfers often occurred shortly after the accumulation of the cash deposits. The largest single outbound transfer that followed the deposits was $202,783.80.

The counterparties for these outbound transfers included entities such as Driftwood Logistics Holdings Ltd., Orchard Gate Ventures Enterprises LLC, and Thistledown Commodities Partners LP. The nature of the relationship between Benedict Tillingham and these entities could not be readily established from the account documentation or the transaction details. The outward flow of funds, particularly in amounts disproportionate to the historical activity, indicated a potential shift in the purpose or utilization of the account.

The transaction monitoring system’s alert generation was further supported by observations recorded by frontline staff. Teller line interactions indicated that Benedict Tillingham had inquired about currency transaction reporting thresholds on multiple occasions. These inquiries, coupled with the pattern of sub-threshold deposits, suggested an awareness of the regulatory requirements and a deliberate effort to structure transactions to avoid reporting.

The combination of these factors—the substantial increase in cash volume, the structuring of deposits below the reporting threshold, the practice of branch rotation, the subsequent large outbound transfers, and the inquiries regarding reporting requirements—represented a fundamental departure from the expected account activity. The statistical baseline for Account 34-72893-3 was exceeded by orders of magnitude, and the nature of the transactions shifted from routine personal and business expenses to high-velocity cash processing and large-value funds transfers. The activity during the review period was inconsistent with the established customer profile and the historical pattern of behavior.

## Account Profile and Baseline Activity - Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC

Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC established account 88-53482-2 at Cortex Bank and Trust on May 12, 2021. The account was opened as a standard commercial checking product intended to support the subject’s stated business model of facilitating cross-border trade and logistics management. Account opening documentation identified Beatriz Zimmerman and Benedict Tillingham as the primary beneficial owners, each holding a forty percent interest, with Séverin Castellanos and Philippa Ashworth listed as non-owner authorized signers. The documented source of funds at account inception was a mid-five-figure initial deposit via wire transfer originating from Cedarline Ventures Corp. The customer profile completed at onboarding indicated anticipated monthly transaction volumes consisting of several dozen incoming and outgoing wire transfers, with an expected average monthly credit volume in the mid-six figures. The profile explicitly stated that cash handling was not an anticipated feature of the business model, and no cash limits or special handling instructions were requested or established.

During the first eighteen months of the account’s history, activity was generally consistent with the established profile. Monthly credit volumes fluctuated between the low and mid-six figures, primarily composed of domestic and international wire transfers from entities such as Driftwood Logistics Holdings Ltd. and Orchard Gate Ventures Enterprises LLC. Debit activity was similarly dominated by outgoing wire transfers to commercial counterparties, including Thistledown Commodities Partners LP and Cascadia Consulting Corp., alongside routine operational expenses such as payroll and vendor payments. Cash activity during this period was negligible, consisting only of occasional, low-dollar withdrawals for petty cash purposes, rarely exceeding a few hundred dollars in any given month. The statistical baseline maintained by the transaction monitoring system reflected this pattern, establishing an expected cash deposit volume of zero and triggering an alert only if aggregate monthly cash deposits exceeded a de minimis threshold.

A marked shift in the account’s transaction profile occurred approximately six months prior to the commencement of the current review period. Beginning in June 2023, the account began to receive intermittent cash deposits. These initial deposits were relatively small, typically in the low four figures, and were interspersed among the established pattern of wire transfers. While this represented a deviation from the stated business model, the volume remained below the threshold that would trigger automated alerts based on the established statistical baseline. However, the frequency and magnitude of these cash deposits steadily increased throughout the third and fourth quarters of 2023. By November 2023, the monthly cash deposit volume had grown to represent a significant minority of the account’s total incoming funds, averaging in the low five figures per month. This escalation in cash activity prompted an initial review by the relationship manager, who documented a conversation with Beatriz Zimmerman in which she attributed the change to a new client base that preferred settling invoices in cash. The relationship manager noted this explanation but did not formally request an update to the customer profile or the statistical baseline.

The onset of the current review period on December 18, 2023, coincided with a dramatic acceleration in the observed cash activity, fundamentally altering the account’s risk profile. The previously established pattern of wire transfers became increasingly marginalized as cash deposits emerged as the primary source of incoming funds. Over the course of the review period, the aggregate cash volume deposited into account 88-53482-2 reached $899,468.70. This figure represents a profound departure from the historical baseline, exceeding the previously anticipated zero cash volume by an order of magnitude that cannot be reconciled with the stated business model or the explanation previously provided to the relationship manager.

The statistical anomaly is further highlighted by the specific characteristics of the cash deposits. Unlike the intermittent, low-dollar cash activity observed prior to the review period, the activity during the review period was characterized by a high frequency of substantial cash deposits. The monitoring system recorded numerous instances where the aggregate daily cash deposits approached, but did not exceed, the $10,000 regulatory reporting threshold. This pattern of sustained, high-volume cash activity is fundamentally inconsistent with a business model focused on cross-border trade and logistics, sectors where electronic funds transfers are the industry standard for commercial settlements. The sheer volume of cash being introduced into the account, far exceeding any reasonable expectation for operational petty cash or incidental retail transactions, suggests a significant change in the nature of the business operations or the introduction of an undisclosed revenue stream.

The departure from the baseline is not solely quantifiable by the aggregate volume but also by the velocity and structure of the transactions. Prior to the review period, funds entering the account typically remained on deposit for several days or weeks before being disbursed, reflecting normal business cash flow management. During the review period, the account exhibited a high velocity of funds, with the substantial cash deposits often being rapidly depleted by outgoing electronic transfers. This rapid transit of funds, particularly when the incoming funds are in the form of cash and the outgoing funds are electronic, is a recognized indicator of potential money laundering activity, specifically the placement and layering phases. The reviewing analyst noted that the largest single outbound transfer that followed the deposits during the review period was $202,783.80, a transaction that occurred within forty-eight hours of a series of substantial cash deposits. This rapid conversion of physical currency into electronic funds and subsequent transfer to third parties represents a significant escalation in risk compared to the account’s historical activity.

The monitoring system’s statistical baseline, which had been calibrated based on the account’s initial eighteen months of operation, proved inadequate to capture the evolving risk profile prior to the dramatic escalation in December 2023. The gradual increase in cash activity throughout late 2023 highlights the limitations of static baselines in detecting slow-moving typologies. However, the activity observed during the review period represents a complete rupture with the established baseline, rendering the original customer profile obsolete and necessitating a comprehensive reassessment of the account’s purpose and the source of its funds. The introduction of nearly a million dollars in cash over an eleven-month period into an account that was explicitly established with the expectation of zero cash handling is the central anomaly that drives this investigation. The reviewing analyst determined that the account’s current activity profile is unrecognizable from its historical baseline and cannot be substantiated by the documented business purpose.

## Customer Due Diligence File Review - Beatriz Zimmerman

A review of the customer due diligence file for Beatriz Zimmerman was conducted to assess the adequacy and currency of the information held by Cortex Bank and Trust. The file review aimed to determine if the documented profile aligned with the observed transaction activity in account 57-21534-1 during the review period spanning December 18, 2023, through November 1, 2024. The assessment focused on the completeness of identification records, the presence and validity of source of funds and source of wealth corroboration, and the status of ongoing monitoring requirements.

The identification documentation on file for Beatriz Zimmerman consisted of a state-issued driver's license. The copy retained by Cortex Bank and Trust was legible, and the identification was current at the time of account opening. A secondary form of identification, a utility bill establishing residential address, was also present and dated within the required timeframe prior to account inception. The information recorded on the identification documents matched the details recorded in the core banking system. No discrepancies concerning the customer's identity or physical address were noted during the review of the primary identification records.

As the subject account, 57-21534-1, is held by an individual, beneficial ownership certification forms are not applicable. The account is established as a personal checking account, and Beatriz Zimmerman is the sole authorized signer and account owner. There was no documentation suggesting any secondary authorized users or powers of attorney associated with the account. The file did not contain any indications that the account was intended for business purposes or that the customer operated a sole proprietorship through this specific account.

The documented source of funds information was reviewed to ascertain the anticipated nature and volume of transactional activity. The account opening documentation indicated that the primary source of funds would be salary and wages from employment. The customer listed an occupation as an administrative assistant at a local logistics firm. The anticipated monthly deposit volume recorded in the profile was a low four-figure sum, consistent with the stated occupation. The file did not contain any documentation, such as recent pay stubs or tax returns, to substantiate the stated income or provide further detail on the source of wealth. The customer profile did not anticipate significant cash deposit activity, nor did it indicate that the customer would engage in frequent, high-value wire transfers.

The observed transaction activity diverged significantly from the anticipated activity documented in the customer profile. The aggregate cash volume deposited into account 57-21534-1 during the review period amounted to $899,468.70. This volume is entirely inconsistent with the stated source of funds and the anticipated monthly deposit volume recorded at account opening. The file contained no subsequent updates or notes explaining the significant increase in cash activity. There was no documentation to suggest a change in employment, receipt of an inheritance, sale of a significant asset, or any other legitimate event that would account for the influx of cash.

The due diligence file review also assessed the presence of any documentary exceptions or outstanding information requests. The review confirmed that there were no pending requests for updated identification or further clarification regarding the account's purpose. The file appeared administratively complete based on the requirements at the time of account opening. However, the lack of updated information regarding the source of the substantial cash deposits represents a significant gap in understanding the customer's financial profile.

The date of the last periodic review of the customer profile was noted. The review was conducted prior to the commencement of the current review period. The notes from the previous review indicated that the account was functioning as expected, with activity primarily consisting of payroll direct deposits and routine consumer expenditures. The previous review did not identify any unusual or suspicious activity, and the risk rating assigned to the customer remained unchanged at that time. The significant deviation from the anticipated activity occurred subsequent to the last periodic review.

Further analysis of the customer file was undertaken to identify any connections to the other subjects or related businesses involved in the investigation. The file for Beatriz Zimmerman did not contain any documented links to Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC, Benedict Tillingham, Séverin Castellanos, or Philippa Ashworth. There was no indication in the account opening documents or subsequent profile updates that the customer had any affiliation with Driftwood Logistics Holdings Ltd., Orchard Gate Ventures Enterprises LLC, Thistledown Commodities Partners LP, Cascadia Consulting Corp., Quarrystone Textiles Inc., Cedarline Ventures Corp., or Fairmount Holdings Partners LP. The absence of documented connections in the due diligence file contrasts with the transactional linkages identified during the broader investigation.

The review of the due diligence file highlights a significant disparity between the documented customer profile and the actual transactional behavior observed in account 57-21534-1. The stated occupation and anticipated account activity provide no legitimate explanation for the aggregate cash deposits of $899,468.70. The lack of corroborating documentation regarding the source of these funds, coupled with the absence of any documented relationship to the other subjects or related entities, presents a material inconsistency. The file, while administratively complete at the time of account opening, lacks the necessary information to rationalize the significant influx of cash and subsequent outbound transfers. The due diligence information held by Cortex Bank and Trust for Beatriz Zimmerman does not support the observed transactional activity and fails to establish a legitimate economic purpose for the movement of these funds.

## Prior Alert and Disposition History - Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC

A review of the monitoring history for Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC, account 88-53482-2, was conducted as part of the current investigation. The customer relationship has generated multiple alerts since the account was opened. The disposition history of these prior alerts was evaluated to determine if previous analytical conclusions remain supportable given the activity identified during the current review period, which spans December 18, 2023, through November 1, 2024. The evaluation indicated that several prior alerts were closed without filing a Suspicious Activity Report based on rationales that are challenged by the findings of the current investigation.

An alert was generated on December 20, 2023, triggered by a scenario designed to detect frequent cash deposits falling just below the $10,000 threshold for Currency Transaction Reporting. The alert captured a series of deposits into the Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC account over the preceding five business days. The reviewing analyst documented that the business model, as stated during account onboarding, involved significant cash receipts from retail sales of specialized goods. The analyst concluded that the deposit sizes, which generally ranged from several thousand dollars to just under the reporting threshold, were consistent with the expected cash flow of the business. The alert was closed on December 26, 2023, with no further action. The reviewing analyst noted that the customer had provided a plausible explanation for the cash volume, and no immediate onward transmission of funds was observed at that time.

In light of the current investigation, the disposition of the December 20, 2023 alert appears to have been premature. The current review identified a sustained pattern of deposits clustered closely below the regulatory reporting threshold. Specifically, deposits of $8,861.79, $8,402.48, and $9,344.10 were recorded in quick succession. While the initial alert captured only the beginning of this pattern, the analyst's reliance on the stated business model without requiring further substantiation of the specific deposit amounts failed to account for the possibility of deliberate structuring. The subsequent volume of cash deposited during the current review period, totaling $899,468.70, significantly exceeds the anticipated cash flow documented at onboarding, rendering the initial rationalization unsupportable.

A second alert was generated on January 2, 2024. This alert was triggered by a scenario designed to detect rapid movement of funds, specifically capturing cash deposits that were immediately followed by outbound electronic transfers of similar aggregate amounts. The alert detailed activity occurring between December 27, 2023, and December 29, 2023. The reviewing analyst documented that the outbound transfers were directed to entities identified as suppliers, including Driftwood Logistics Holdings Ltd. and Orchard Gate Ventures Enterprises LLC. The analyst concluded that the activity represented a typical business cycle of receiving cash from sales and immediately remitting payment for inventory or services. The alert was closed on January 4, 2024, with the analyst citing the apparent legitimate business purpose of the counterparties.

The disposition of the January 2, 2024 alert is now assessed as flawed. The current investigation revealed that the outbound transfers were not commensurate with the expected operational expenses of Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC. The initial analysis failed to adequately scrutinize the relationship between the cash deposits and the subsequent wire transfers. The current review established that the rapid outflow of funds, including a single outbound transfer of $202,783.80, often occurred on the same day as the cash deposits. This velocity of funds movement, particularly when involving significant cash deposits, is inconsistent with standard business practices and suggests an intent to obscure the origin of the funds before rapid dissemination. The prior analyst's reliance on the names of the counterparties without verifying the economic substance of the underlying transactions contributed to an incorrect assessment of the risk.

A third alert, generated outside the current review period, was triggered by a scenario monitoring for unusual branch utilization. The alert captured multiple deposits made to the Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC account at different Cortex Bank and Trust branches on the same business day. The reviewing analyst noted that the business operated a mobile sales force and concluded that the deposits at various branches reflected the geographic distribution of the sales representatives. The analyst contacted the relationship manager, who corroborated this explanation. The alert was closed without filing, based on the determination that the activity was consistent with the known operational footprint of the business.

While the geographic explanation for branch rotation may have appeared plausible in isolation, it is inconsistent with the broader pattern of activity identified during the current review. The current investigation found that the branch rotation was frequently employed on days when multiple sub-threshold cash deposits were made. This suggests that the use of multiple branches was not merely a convenience for a mobile workforce, but rather a deliberate tactic to avoid detection by branch personnel and to mitigate the risk of a Currency Transaction Report being filed for aggregated daily cash transactions exceeding $10,000. The prior analyst's failure to consider the branch rotation in conjunction with the size and frequency of the cash deposits led to a misinterpretation of the behavior.

A review of customer interactions documented in the core banking system revealed that inquiries regarding reporting thresholds were made by representatives of Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC at the teller line on December 18, 2023, and December 25, 2023. These inquiries were not flagged by the automated monitoring system and were therefore not considered during the disposition of the prior alerts. The current investigation incorporates these documented inquiries, which provide critical context for the subsequent deposit patterns. The relationship manager reminded Ashworth that Cortex Bank and Trust requires adequate documentation to support the transaction activity in her account and that failure to provide such documentation could result in account closure. Ashworth assured the relationship manager that she was doing her best to gather the necessary paperwork.

On January 4, 2024, the reviewing analyst reviewed the information gathered from the relationship manager and the branch manager. The analyst noted significant discrepancies between Ashworth’s explanations and the transaction record. Ashworth’s claim that the deposits represented daily retail receipts was inconsistent with the clustered amounts and the frequent branch rotation. Furthermore, her inability to provide documentation for the outbound transfers, particularly the large transfer of $202,783.80, raised concerns regarding the legitimacy of her stated business purposes. The analyst concluded that Ashworth’s explanations were insufficient to mitigate the red flags identified in the transaction activity. The analyst noted that the customer’s behavior at the teller line, specifically her inquiries about reporting thresholds and subsequent adjustments to her deposits, was highly indicative of an intent to evade Currency Transaction Report requirements. The analyst also noted that the immediate transfer of funds following the cash deposits was consistent with layering, a common money laundering typology. The lack of substantiating documentation for the source of funds and the purpose of the transfers further compounded the suspicious nature of the activity. The reviewing analyst determined that the information obtained through the interviews did not provide a legitimate business rationale for the observed transaction patterns in account 36-56838-5.

## Key Finding

The review established that Beatriz Zimmerman was structuring cash deposits to evade currency transaction reporting requirements, a conclusion supported by the identification of a previously undisclosed, high-value transfer. While the initial investigation focused on the aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period, the determinative finding occurred when the reviewing analyst traced the ultimate disposition of the structured funds. The analysis revealed that on October 10, 2024, a consolidation of the sub-threshold deposits was executed, resulting in a single outbound wire transfer. This transfer, totaling $465,028.48, was directed to an external account held by Cyrus Cárdenas. The funds were routed from account 59-11704-9, which had acted as a temporary holding account for the accumulated cash deposits. The customer was unable to substantiate a legitimate business purpose for this transfer or the relationship with the beneficiary, indicating the structured deposits were orchestrated specifically to fund this transaction.

## Applicable Policy and Regulatory Reference

The activity described in this report, specifically regarding the account held by Séverin Castellanos, was reviewed in accordance with Cortex Bank and Trust's obligations under the Bank Secrecy Act and related anti-money laundering regulations. The Bank Secrecy Act requires financial institutions to report suspicious activity that might signal criminal activity, including money laundering, tax evasion, or other financial crimes. This obligation is central to the bank's role in safeguarding the financial system and ensuring that its services are not utilized for illicit purposes. A key component of this regulatory framework is the requirement to identify and report transactions that appear designed to evade reporting requirements, a practice commonly known as structuring. Structuring involves breaking down larger, reportable transactions into smaller, sub-threshold amounts to avoid triggering the filing of a Currency Transaction Report. The regulatory threshold for filing a Currency Transaction Report is established at $10,000 in cash transactions, either deposited or withdrawn, by or on behalf of the same person on a single business day. Transactions that appear to be deliberately sized or timed to stay below this $10,000 threshold are considered suspicious and necessitate further investigation and potential reporting.

Cortex Bank and Trust maintains comprehensive internal policies and procedures designed to detect, investigate, and report suspicious activity in compliance with these regulatory requirements. The bank's transaction monitoring systems are calibrated to identify patterns of activity that deviate from expected customer behavior or that align with known money laundering typologies. These systems alert analysts to potential instances of structuring, such as frequent cash deposits just below the $10,000 reporting threshold, multiple deposits across different branches on the same day, or other unusual cash handling practices. The internal policies require that alerts generated by the transaction monitoring system be reviewed by designated analysts within the Financial Intelligence Unit. Analysts are tasked with evaluating the alerts in the context of the customer's profile, historical account activity, and known business or personal circumstances to determine if the activity is suspicious or if there is a reasonable explanation.

The review of the activity associated with Séverin Castellanos's account was initiated following the generation of alerts indicative of potential structuring. The internal escalation policy dictates that when an analyst identifies activity that cannot be reasonably explained by the customer's known profile and that exhibits characteristics of structuring, the matter must be escalated for a more in-depth investigation. This investigation process involves a comprehensive review of the customer's account history, including the frequency, volume, and nature of the transactions, as well as an assessment of any counterparty relationships. The policy also requires analysts to consider contextual factors, such as the customer's occupation, the expected source of funds, and any interactions the customer may have had with bank personnel regarding reporting requirements. The bank's policies emphasize the importance of identifying and documenting red flags, which are specific behaviors or transaction patterns that suggest a higher risk of illicit activity.

In the context of cash transactions, red flags that are specifically addressed in the bank's training and policy documents include deposits clustered just below the $10,000 threshold, the use of multiple branches to conduct transactions on the same day, and customer inquiries about reporting requirements. The policies guide analysts to consider the cumulative effect of multiple red flags when assessing the overall suspicion level of the activity. The internal procedures also outline the requirements for documenting the investigation findings, including the rationale for any determination of suspicion. This documentation must be thorough and objective, avoiding speculation and relying on factual observations of the account activity. The policies further stipulate that if the investigation concludes that the activity is suspicious, a Suspicious Activity Report must be filed within the timeframe mandated by regulation. The internal threshold for filing a Suspicious Activity Report when a suspect can be identified is $5,000.

The activity observed in the account of Séverin Castellanos included cash deposits that were clustered in amounts that approached, but did not exceed, the $10,000 Currency Transaction Report threshold. The investigation noted multiple instances where deposits were made in amounts such as $8,861.79 and $9,344.10. Another observed deposit was in the amount of $8,402.48. The bank's policies regarding structuring identification require analysts to view these sub-threshold deposits not in isolation, but as part of a potential pattern. The policies direct analysts to look for related activity, such as rapid depletion of funds following the deposits or the use of multiple channels to deposit funds. The investigation into the account held by Séverin Castellanos noted that the cash deposits were frequently followed by outbound transfers, including a large single outbound transfer of $202,783.80. The policies governing suspicious activity reporting require that the analysis consider the entire sequence of transactions to determine if the overall pattern lacks an apparent lawful purpose or is not the sort in which the particular customer would normally be expected to engage.

The bank's internal guidelines also require a review of any interactions between the customer and branch personnel that might provide context for the transaction activity. The policies state that inquiries by a customer regarding the bank's reporting thresholds or requests to alter a transaction after being informed of the reporting requirements are strong indicators of potential structuring intent. The investigation process requires that any such interactions be documented and factored into the overall assessment of the activity. The policies emphasize that the determination of suspicion is a judgment based on the totality of the circumstances, including the transaction patterns, the customer's profile, and any associated red flags. The regulatory framework and the bank's corresponding internal policies are designed to ensure that potential instances of structuring are identified, thoroughly investigated, and reported to the appropriate authorities when the activity cannot be reasonably explained as legitimate financial behavior. The investigation into the account of Séverin Castellanos was conducted in accordance with these established procedures and regulatory requirements.

## Internal Escalation and Committee Deliberation

The activity observed on the account held by Beatriz Zimmerman prompted an internal escalation to the Suspicious Activity Review Committee. This escalation originated from a senior investigator within the Financial Intelligence Unit on November 10, 2024, following a comprehensive review of the customer's transaction history during the defined review period. The investigator's referral memorandum highlighted the pattern of cash deposits, noting that the aggregate volume of cash deposited, totalling $899,468.70, was significantly inconsistent with the customer's stated occupation and expected account activity as documented at onboarding. The referral further emphasized the clustering of these deposits in amounts just below the $10,000 regulatory reporting threshold, a pattern strongly suggestive of structuring to evade Currency Transaction Report filings.

The Suspicious Activity Review Committee convened on November 15, 2024, to deliberate on the escalation. The committee, comprised of senior representatives from Compliance, the Financial Intelligence Unit, and Retail Banking, reviewed the investigator's findings and the supporting documentation. The primary focus of the deliberation was to determine whether the observed activity met the regulatory threshold for filing a Suspicious Activity Report. The committee considered the specific nature of the deposits, acknowledging the investigator's assertion that the frequency and amounts of the cash deposits were highly unusual for an individual account. The committee members reviewed the transaction logs detailing the multiple sub-threshold deposits, including the specific instances where the customer made deposits of $8,861.79, $8,402.48, and $9,344.10. These transactions, executed in close proximity to one another, were identified as key indicators of potential structuring.

During the committee meeting, a representative from Retail Banking raised a question regarding the customer's potential legitimate source of cash. The representative suggested that the customer might be operating an undisclosed cash-intensive business or perhaps acting as an informal agent for a community group, which could theoretically explain the high volume of cash. This suggestion prompted a review of the account's Know Your Customer profile. The review confirmed that the customer had not declared any business ownership or affiliation that would justify such substantial cash deposits. The committee noted that even if an undisclosed business existed, the deliberate structuring of the deposits to avoid reporting thresholds remained a significant concern and a potential violation of the Bank Secrecy Act.

The committee also discussed the subsequent movement of funds following the cash deposits. The investigation had revealed that the cash deposits were frequently followed by rapid, large-scale outbound transfers, often in amounts corresponding to the recently deposited cash. The committee reviewed the details of the largest single outbound transfer, which amounted to $202,783.80. The rapid dissipation of funds, particularly when coupled with the structured cash deposits, was viewed by the committee as a classic indicator of money laundering activity, specifically the placement and layering phases. The committee debated whether the outbound transfers provided any further clarity on the nature of the funds, but concluded that the destinations of the transfers did not offer a readily apparent legitimate explanation for the initial cash deposits.

A dissenting view was briefly articulated by a compliance officer who questioned whether the evidence of structuring was definitive. The officer noted that while the deposit amounts were clustered below the threshold, there were no documented instances of the customer explicitly asking tellers about reporting limits or attempting to alter a transaction after being informed of the requirement for a Currency Transaction Report. The officer suggested that the customer might simply prefer to keep a certain amount of cash on hand and only deposit the excess when it approached $10,000. However, this argument was countered by the Financial Intelligence Unit representative, who pointed to the sheer volume of the aggregate deposits and the frequency of the sub-threshold transactions. The representative argued that the consistency of the pattern over the review period, combined with the lack of a plausible legitimate source, strongly outweighed the possibility of coincidental behavior.

The committee's deliberation then focused on the customer's use of multiple branch locations. The investigation had highlighted instances where the customer executed transactions at different branches on the same day or within a short timeframe. The committee recognized this branch rotation as a common tactic employed by individuals attempting to obscure their overall transaction volume and evade detection by branch staff. The committee agreed that this behavior, when viewed in conjunction with the structured deposit amounts, significantly strengthened the case for a Suspicious Activity Report filing. The committee members concluded that the combination of these factors presented a compelling picture of deliberate attempts to circumvent regulatory reporting requirements.

Following the discussion, the committee members voted on the proposed action. The consensus reached was that the activity observed in the account held by Beatriz Zimmerman was highly suspicious and warranted the filing of a Suspicious Activity Report. The committee determined that the pattern of cash deposits, the aggregate volume of those deposits, the rapid subsequent outbound transfers, and the customer's use of multiple branch locations collectively demonstrated a clear attempt to evade Currency Transaction Report filings and potentially launder illicit funds. The decision to file was unanimous among the voting members, with the initial dissenting view ultimately withdrawn after further consideration of the aggregate data.

The committee formally recorded its decision to file a Suspicious Activity Report and directed the Financial Intelligence Unit to proceed with the drafting and submission of the narrative. The committee also recommended that the relationship manager for the account be notified of the filing, albeit with strict instructions not to disclose the filing to the customer, in accordance with anti-tipping-off regulations. Furthermore, the committee instructed the Financial Intelligence Unit to conduct a 90-day continuing activity review to monitor the account for any ongoing suspicious behavior. The escalation and deliberation process was documented in the internal case management system, ensuring a clear audit trail of the decision-making process. The committee's findings emphasized that the customer's activity presented a significant compliance risk to Cortex Bank and Trust and required formal notification to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

## Remediation and Account Restriction Actions

Following the completion of the investigation into Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC, account 88-53482-2, the Cortex Bank and Trust Financial Intelligence Unit initiated a series of remediation actions designed to mitigate the risks associated with the observed cash activity. The volume of the aggregate cash deposits during the review period, totaling $899,468.70, combined with the pattern of branch rotation within a single business day and the documented customer questions about reporting thresholds at the teller line, necessitated immediate intervention to limit the potential for further structuring and to ensure the bank's compliance with Bank Secrecy Act obligations. The primary focus of these actions was to control the cash handling capabilities of Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC while a broader relationship review was conducted.

The initial step in the remediation process involved the imposition of a hard cash deposit restriction on account 88-53482-2. This restriction was implemented systemically, preventing teller personnel across all Cortex Bank and Trust branches from accepting cash deposits into the account. The decision to apply a hard restriction rather than a soft warning was driven by the persistent nature of the sub-threshold deposits, such as the transactions of $8,861.79, $8,402.48, and $9,344.10, which appeared calculated to avoid the $10,000 currency transaction reporting requirement. The restriction was communicated to branch management, with explicit instructions that any attempts by representatives of Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC, including Beatriz Zimmerman or Benedict Tillingham, to deposit cash should be refused and immediately reported to the Financial Intelligence Unit.

Concurrently, a review of the account's channel access was undertaken. Given the observed pattern of cash deposits being immediately followed by same-amount outbound transfers, the decision was made to restrict the account's access to external wire transfer capabilities. The largest single outbound transfer that followed the deposits, an amount of $202,783.80, highlighted the velocity with which funds were being moved out of the institution following their introduction in cash form. By disabling wire origination privileges, the bank aimed to disrupt this rapid movement of funds, ensuring that any balances generated by other deposit methods remained within the account for a sufficient period to allow for adequate monitoring and clearance. The restriction on wire transfers was applied to both online banking channels and in-branch requests.

In addition to the transactional restrictions, the Financial Intelligence Unit applied a series of enhanced monitoring rules to the profile of Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC. These rules were configured to generate alerts for any activity that deviated from the restricted parameters or that resembled the previously observed patterns. Specifically, the monitoring was calibrated to identify any attempts to circumvent the cash deposit restriction through the use of automated teller machines or night drop facilities, although these channels are generally not permitted for high-volume commercial cash deposits at Cortex Bank and Trust. The rules were also designed to monitor the source of non-cash deposits, such as checks or electronic transfers, to ensure that the restriction on cash was not simply displacing the activity into other, potentially less transparent, forms of value transfer.

The relationship management team responsible for Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC was formally notified of the restrictions and the underlying concerns regarding the structuring activity. The relationship manager was instructed to contact the authorized signers on the account to inform them of the limitations placed on their cash handling and wire transfer capabilities. The communication was required to be neutral in tone, citing general risk management policies and the need for updated due diligence documentation, without disclosing the specific nature of the suspicious activity investigation or the filing of a Suspicious Activity Report. The relationship manager was also tasked with obtaining a detailed explanation for the cash intensive nature of the business, particularly given the stated business line of Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC, which typically does not involve significant cash receipts.

A formal relationship review was convened, involving representatives from the Financial Intelligence Unit, the commercial banking division, and the bank's legal counsel. The review committee examined the findings of the investigation, focusing on the substantial aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period, the pattern of sub-threshold deposits, and the rapid outward movement of funds. The committee considered the risk profile of Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC against the bank's risk appetite and the potential compliance implications of maintaining the relationship. The failure of the customer to provide a coherent business rationale for the cash activity, coupled with the observed attempts to evade reporting thresholds, weighed heavily in the committee's deliberations.

The relationship review committee ultimately determined that the risks associated with Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC exceeded the bank's tolerance. The decision was made to initiate the process of exiting the relationship. The exit strategy was formulated to minimize disruption to the bank while ensuring that all remaining funds were handled appropriately. The account restrictions, including the prohibition on cash deposits and the limitation on wire transfers, were maintained during the exit period. The customer was provided with a standard notification of the bank's intent to close the account, affording them a reasonable timeframe to make alternative banking arrangements. The notification did not specify the reasons for the closure beyond general policy considerations.

During the exit period, the account remained subject to the enhanced monitoring rules previously implemented. The Financial Intelligence Unit committed to reviewing all transactional activity on account 88-53482-2 until the account balance reached zero and the account was formally closed on the bank's core system. Any significant deviations from expected closing procedures, such as attempts to deposit large sums of non-cash funds or requests for unusual disbursement methods, were flagged for immediate review. The monitoring commitment also extended to the related accounts of Beatriz Zimmerman, Benedict Tillingham, Séverin Castellanos, and Philippa Ashworth, to ensure that the activity observed in the Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC account was not displaced into these personal or affiliated accounts.

The remediation actions taken in response to the activity in account 88-53482-2 represent a comprehensive effort to mitigate the identified risks and protect the bank from potential regulatory exposure. The combination of immediate account restrictions, enhanced monitoring, and the ultimate decision to exit the relationship demonstrates a proactive approach to managing the risks associated with suspected structuring. The Financial Intelligence Unit will continue to monitor the progress of the account closure and will maintain the enhanced scrutiny on the related individuals and entities until the exit process is complete and the risk is fully extinguished. The documentation of these actions, along with the underlying investigation findings, will be retained in accordance with the bank's recordkeeping policies and will be available for review by authorized regulatory personnel.

## Law Enforcement Coordination and Information Sharing

On January 4, 2024, Cortex Bank and Trust received a formal written request from a federal law enforcement agency concerning the financial activities of Benedict Tillingham and the associated account 34-72893-3. The request sought specific transaction records and account documentation for the period beginning December 18, 2023. Cortex Bank and Trust complied with this request, providing statements, deposit slips, and images of cleared items related to the specified account. The provided documentation included records of the aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period, which totaled $899,468.70.

Following the receipt of the initial law enforcement request, the reviewing analyst identified a pattern of cash deposits into account 34-72893-3 that appeared structured to evade currency transaction reporting requirements. Specifically, multiple cash deposits were observed in amounts ranging from $9,719.68 to $8,917.00. For example, a deposit of $8,861.79 was made on December 26, 2023, followed by a deposit of $8,402.48 on December 27, 2023, and a deposit of $9,344.10 on December 28, 2023. These deposits were often followed by immediate outbound transfers in corresponding amounts. The largest single outbound transfer observed following a series of these deposits was for $202,783.80.

In response to these findings, Cortex Bank and Trust initiated a Section 314(b) information sharing request on January 2, 2024. The request was directed to another financial institution where Benedict Tillingham was known to hold an account. The purpose of this request was to gather additional information regarding his financial activities, particularly any transactions that might be related to the suspected structuring observed at Cortex Bank and Trust. The response received from the other institution indicated that they had also observed a pattern of cash deposits in amounts slightly below the $10,000 threshold, followed by immediate outbound transfers.

The reviewing analyst noted that the branch rotation within a single business day and the customer's inquiries about reporting thresholds at the teller line, as documented in the case file, further supported the suspicion of structuring. These factors, combined with the pattern of sub-threshold cash deposits and subsequent immediate outbound transfers, suggested a deliberate effort to avoid currency transaction reporting requirements.

Cortex Bank and Trust provided the findings of its internal investigation, including the information obtained through the Section 314(b) request, to the federal law enforcement agency that had initiated the initial inquiry. This information was shared in accordance with applicable laws and regulations governing the disclosure of financial information to law enforcement authorities. The bank continues to monitor the activity in account 34-72893-3 and will provide any further information or documentation requested by law enforcement in connection with this matter.

The reviewing analyst also identified connections between Benedict Tillingham and other individuals and businesses involved in the suspected structuring activity. For instance, Beatriz Zimmerman (account 57-21534-1), Cedarline Exports Enterprises LLC (account 88-53482-2), Séverin Castellanos (account 15-57913-4), and Philippa Ashworth (account 36-56838-5) were all observed making similar sub-threshold cash deposits, often accompanied by branch rotation and immediate outbound transfers. These individuals and businesses were also found to have transactions with counterparties such as Driftwood Logistics Holdings Ltd., Orchard Gate Ventures Enterprises LLC, Thistledown Commodities Partners LP, Cascadia Consulting Corp., Quarrystone Textiles Inc., Cedarline Ventures Corp., and Fairmount Holdings Partners LP.

The connections between these individuals, businesses, and counterparties suggest a broader network involved in the suspected structuring activity. The reviewing analyst has documented these connections and will continue to investigate any further links or patterns that may emerge. The information gathered regarding these related individuals and businesses will be shared with law enforcement authorities as appropriate, in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.

The reviewing analyst has also noted that the suspected structuring activity appears to have been ongoing for several months, with the aggregate cash volume deposited during the review period totaling $899,468.70. This significant volume of cash deposits, combined with the other red flags observed, further supports the suspicion of deliberate evasion of currency transaction reporting requirements. Cortex Bank and Trust remains committed to cooperating with law enforcement authorities in their investigation of this matter and will continue to monitor the accounts involved for any further suspicious activity.
